Chapter Notes

Hi! So I got this idea MONTHS ago when the the HSR April Fool's Chef video said that Phainon had "professional expertise to select premium chicken breeds." You don't need any Stardew knowledge to read this. Phainon's just a country boy with his animals on his ranch with a stupid crush on the city guy who just moved into the old farmhouse nearby.

I also wrote over half of this already so I'll be rolling out updates pretty regularly

Living in a small town, Phainon’s daily life was a repetitive routine. 

He’d wake up at an early hour to the crowing of his roosters, when the sky was still dark and the rest of Aedes Elysiae was still asleep. His boots would be dampened by the morning dew as he tended to the livestock: milking cows, gathering eggs, filling the feeders. By the time he’d finish, the sun would have risen, and his sister would have prepared breakfast for the both of them. They’d chat over the kitchen table until the clock struck 9, and the ranch opened for the day. 

For all his complaining, Phainon loved life in the country. His mornings may be tedious, but they beat a boring office job in the city. Castorice had once asked him if he’d ever thought about leaving the valley, and he’d only snorted in response. He’d never dream of leaving this life behind; he loved it, mud-stained clothes and all. 

Even if some mornings tested his patience. 

“Phainon!” Cyrene called, cheery voice muffled through his bedroom walls. “The festival begins at 9!” 

He groaned. It was only 30 minutes before his normal alarm, but it felt so much earlier. 

He heard Cyrene’s signature exaggerated sigh. “Aren’t you going to defend your title as the Egg Festival champion?”

”It’s not like there’s any competition,” he muttered, although he forced himself to get out of bed. For all his talk, he knew that Castorice wouldn’t hesitate to swipe his champion status right out from under him. She’d almost done it last year.

”Either way, I’ll be leaving at 8:30, with or without you.”

A series of chores and a shower later, Phainon walked alongside his sister to the Town Square. It was the same path he took most days: to run to the general goods store, to hang out at the saloon, to sit on the ocean dock. He’d give a friendly wave to the few people he saw along the way, smiling to himself as they went their separate ways. 

Festival days, though, were entirely different. He attended all of the Valley’s communal events, but he’d still never grown accustomed to the crowds. Regardless, he took it upon himself to scan the sea of people; if he forgot to say hi to Hyacine again, Cyrene would give him an earful that rivaled last year’s. 

He listed off names in his head: Aglaea, Anaxa, Castorice…until he saw someone he didn’t recognize.

”Cyrene?” He asked. “When did tourists start visiting the Egg Festival?” 

“Tourists?” Cyrene sounded equally as confused. “Where?”

“You see him? At the strawberries stand?” Phainon started. “Blond, kinda tall-“

”You mean Mydeimos?” Cyrene asked, amusement creeping into her voice. “Oh, he’s no tourist. He moved in a couple weeks ago from Okhema. I’m surprised you haven't met him yet.”

“Okhema?” Phainon repeated. He watched as the apparently-not-tourist slid some coins across the counter. “Wonder what possessed a city slicker to come to our small town.”

“City slicker?” Cyrene said with a small frown. “That’s a bit harsh, don’t you think?”

”What? It’s not an insult.”

Cyrene opened her mouth to respond-probably a scolding, if Phainon had to guess-but before she could, Mayor Krateros announced that the Annual Egg Hunt was about to start. ”Good luck,” she landed on, and Phainon gave a smile before racing to the center of the town. 

“Cas,” he greeted when he reached his destination. “Just us two this year, huh? Just like last year.”

”Three.” 

Phainon whipped his head around to find the source of the unfamiliar voice, only to see the new city kid- Mydeimos -joining the Valley’s annual tradition. “I don’t believe we’ve met,” he said. “Name’s Mydeimos. And you are?” 

He could feel Mydeimos’ golden eyes bearing into him. “Phainon,” he said. “I run the ranch with my sister, Cyrene.” 

“Ah,” Mydeimos said. “We were bound to be acquainted sooner or later then. I only moved in a couple weeks ago, you see.”

“So I’ve heard. I hope you don’t feel too attached to the idea of winning the Egg Hunt. You have no idea just how many years of practice Cas and I have.”

“I’ll make sure to work my hardest to surprise you then.” 

Phainon wanted to say something, but Krateros made his way into the center of the three contestants. He went through the same rules Phainon had heard year after year-no roughhousing with each other, no sabotaging other contestants, and to have fun. He wasn’t listening; instead, he was scouting out his surroundings, planning the best path to take while he waited for the Mayor’s whistle to sound.

When he heard the shrill noise, he broke into a run. He passed the saloon, collecting the colorful eggs scattered around the shrubbery and slipping them into the woven basket on his arm. The seconds slipped by; he counted down in his head, determination to keep his title fueling him. 

The Mayor’s whistle blew when his inner countdown hit zero. Perfect. 

He walked confidently back to the town center, basket dangling by his side. “So? How’d you do?” 

“I don’t think I beat you, if that’s what you’re asking,” Castorice said. “Both you and Mydeimos were running around like maniacs. I stood no chance.”

“Don’t sell yourself short, Cas,” Phainon insisted. He looked around quickly before adding, “you can beat a city slicker any day.” 

Castorice raised an eyebrow. “Is there something I don’t know about? There seems to be some…tension between the two of you.”

“We only met today. Does it really seem like we have a feud going on?” 

“Mostly on your end,” she answered honestly. “He doesn’t seem to hold any hostility.”

Phainon wanted to retort-tell her that he did not hold hostility toward Mydeimos, that it was just common sense that he and Castorice would be better at the Valley’s annual competitions-but he saw Mydeimos nearing them, and the risk of him being within earshot was too great. “It’s nothing,” he settled for instead.

Castorice gave him a look that said we will be discussing this later , before greeting Mydeimos as he stepped in next to Phainon. “Welcome back.” 

“Thank you.” 

Now that the contest wasn’t looming over his head, Phainon could really get a look at him. Mydeimos’ blond hair was dyed red at the tips, his bangs currently clinging to his skin from sweat. The bright tattoos that ran up his arms and neck ended by one of his searing yellow eyes…and if his own weren’t deceiving him, he spotted eyeliner adorning his face. 

He didn’t fit Phainon’s definition of a typical, snotty, city boy.

“Castorice, Mydeimos, and Phainon,” the Mayor began. “Please place your baskets ahead so we can begin the judging process.”

Phainon swore he heard Mydeimos mutter a sarcastic so formal under his breath, and frowned. Even if he didn’t look the part, he sported some of that signature Holy City snarkiness. Looks could be deceiving , he thought to himself as he handed his collection over to Krateros. 

A few minutes passed as the older man counted the contestants’ eggs. Phainon stood idly, hearing murmuring from the audience. He wasn’t sure what for; the Egg Hunt had ended the same way for over half a decade, and they knew what to expect.

”And the winner of this year’s Annual Egg Hunt…”

Phainon took his first step forward, ready to claim his prize.

“…is our new farmer in town, Mydeimos!”

He stopped dead in his tracks. What? 

For a moment Phainon thought that he may have heard incorrectly, but the clapping from the small crowd as Mydeimos took his award snapped him out of it. He’d been beaten. By an Okheman . 

“Seems like the overconfident one wasn’t me, but you.” 

Phainon scowled. Mydeimos was gloating ; his upbringing was clear as day now. And to think Castorice, his best friend, said that he was the one being hostile!

”Whatever,” he grumbled, unable to think of a snide remark. He didn’t look, but he knew the man had to be wearing the most insufferable smile. Befitting for a city kid like him. 

***

“Cyrene, are you sure you didn’t see him cheating?”

Cyrene rolled her eyes as she set Phainon’s plate in front of him. “Yes, I’m sure. You lost, Phainon. It’s okay.”

”He took way longer than Castorice and I to get back to the start,” Phainon insisted. “You can’t tell me that’s not suspicious.”

”Phainon, I know I used the Egg Hunt as an excuse for you to get up this morning, but it’s just a game.”

”That’s exactly what Cas told me.” Phainon mumbled, low enough so his sister wouldn’t hear. 

After the festival had ended, he’d gone over to Castorice’s house to do what they did every year-play Legend of the Prairie King in her bedroom. After over a decade, it felt as much of a custom as the official festival activities; although, without his Egg Champion Status, it felt different than usual.

“What else did she tell you?” Cyrene pulled her chair out and sat down at the table. It turned out that Phainon wasn’t as quiet as he thought.

”She gave me a lecture about ‘judging a book by its cover’ or whatever.” He put down the fork he was holding. “Over this Mydeimos person. Really? I never even said anything bad about the guy!” 

“Even if that were true,” Cyrene said, “you don’t have to voice your opinion for us to know when you dislike someone. It’s written all over your face.” 

Phainon grimaced. He’d asked Castorice if he was bad at controlling his facial expressions, and had been mortified when she’d said “yes” without hesitation; he didn’t appreciate his sister’s reaffirmation.

“Either way, I hope you manage to pull yourself together. Scowling at customers is bad for business.”

“Customers?” Phainon echoed. 

“Yes, customers.” Cyrene spoke through a fork full of food, and Phainon grimaced. “He’s lived here as a farmer for a couple of weeks now. It’s only a matter of time until he grows interested in livestock.” 

“Whatever you say, sis.” Phainon picked up his utensils again. “If he’s as much of a city boy as I think he is, he won’t last two weeks raising chickens.”

“If telling yourself that makes you feel better, then by all means, go ahead,” she said. “Just don’t forget what I said.”

Phainon thought back to the Festival; Mydeimos’ too clean clothes, his snarky words under his breath, those methods that managed to fool both Cas and Cyrene. “I don’t think I’ll have to worry about it for long,” he said. “Guys like him aren’t built lives like ours. It won’t be long until he’s scurrying back to his old, cushy ways.” 

Cyrene rose from her chair, her plate already empty. “I’ll be heading to bed soon,” she said, ignoring what he said. 

“Is it really that late already?” Phainon turned his head to look at the clock, which read 7:30pm.

"No, but I’m exhausted.” She’d taken her ceramic dish to the sink, rinsing it as she spoke. “The combination of a town-wide festival and dealing with an obnoxious younger brother takes a toll on a girl.”

"Okay, I-hey, what do you mean obnoxious younger brother?” 

“Sleep well, lil bro!” Cyrene retreated down the hallway, bedroom door closing behind her.

Obnoxious younger brother , Phainon thought to himself with a scowl. He’d show her.

Chapter End Notes

For all my Stardew players:
Cyrene and Phainon live where Marnie's ranch is, and run the ranch shop
Krateros takes the role of Mayor Lewis
Hyacine is the town doctor
Aglaea runs the general goods store (except she's not as slimy as Pierre. I'd never slander her like that)

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Spring 23, Year 1
chapters.html:
It had taken a little over a week for Mydeimos to show himself in the ranch shop.

Phainon had been running late that morning. One of his cows had kicked the milk pail over, and had splashed the sticky liquid all over his face. The longer shower he’d given himself the liberty of taking had bitten him in the ass; the Okheman boy that had stolen his title was staring right at him, his hair wet and disheveled.

“Speak of the devil,” Cyrene said cheerfully. “This is Phainon-my lovely brother and our local chicken expert.” 

If looks could kill, Phainon’s sister would be dead on the floor.

“No need for introductions, ma’am,” Mydeimos said, with a politeness that almost sounded fake. “We met briefly at the Egg Festival.”

The last two words made Phainon bristle. His politeness was definitely fake , he’d decided.

”Phainon, would you mind? You know more about chickens than I do.” 

Phainon had half a mind to tell her that he did mind. He’d walked in to greet a customer before he’d even had the chance to dry his hair, and was told to give him a lesson on animal care-a lesson that he was sure would be wasted. The moment this guy had to clean up chicken shit, he’d be taking the next bus home. 

Once he’d said it in his head, though…something clicked.

“Of course, sis,” he said, putting on his most charismatic smile. Cyrene had beamed, and Mydeimos had a thinly veiled look of surprise.

It had been a few days since then, and Phainon had spent his middays at Mydeimos’ farm. From the moment he stepped foot onto his land, he scoped it out; determined to find and point out any mistakes he could find.

And he did. He criticized the state of his farmland, and said the state of his harvests were a sorry sight. He emphasized the mess in the chicken coop, acting as if Mydeimos had left it untouched for days. He even commented on his house decorations. Don’t you know? We don’t have furniture like this around here.

Eventually, he knew, Mydeimos would crack. Guys from The Holy City couldn’t handle being told the truth. Even if the truth in this situation was a bit…overexaggerated.

“What’s your problem with me?” Mydeimos asked, hand rested on the chicken coop door. 

Just as expected.

“I don’t have a problem with you,” Phainon said innocently, cocking his head. “I think it’s you that has a problem with me . It’s not my fault you can’t handle constructive criticism.” 

“Constructive criticism, my ass,” Mydeimos said. He backed away from the building. “You’ve done nothing but insult me since the day we met. Is that why you said yes to Cyrene? You wanted a free pass to bully the new guy in town?” 

“ Bullying? ” Phainon echoed. “Is that what you call it in Okhema? Sure, I may have been a little harsh, but-“

“A little harsh.” Mydeimos barked out a laugh. “Sure. You know, I thought that maybe Hephaestion was right. That country folks were close minded and arrogant, thinking they were better than everyone else. But everyone else in the Valley has been nothing but kind to me. You are the only person who has made me feel unwelcome here, Phainon. So what is it?”

Phainon stared at his shoes. Maybe it was the words the new farmer spoke, or the warble with which he said them that made it sound like he wanted to cry. Or maybe it was hearing the familiar clucking of Leghorn Chickens from inside the coop. 

It didn’t matter the reason. Phainon realized he felt… bad . 

”Oh wait. Don’t tell me!” Mydeimos said. “You’re mad that I beat you at that stupid Egg Hunt, aren’t you!”

“That’s not it-“ Phainon started to say, but his words caught in his throat as Mydeimos walked closer to him. He was broad shouldered, only a few inches shorter than Phainon himself-the first person he’d ever met that he didn’t have to lower his head to talk to. 

“Then what is it?” Mydeimos’ gaze was sharp. His eyes seemed to glow when he looked into Phainon’s-a striking shade of gold.

”It’s your…lack of respect,” Phainon landed on. Mydeimos’ eyes narrowed at his lousy defense.

“Lack of respect?” The man got even closer. “Do elaborate, Phainon .”

“Just…how you treat our customs as a joke.” His voice warbled, unconvincing even to his own ears. “Making fun of our…formalities, and such.”

“Is that it, Phainon? Because I only moved here at the beginning of the season. The only festivity I’ve participated in has been the Egg Festival you insisted wasn’t important.”

Fuck. 

“And don’t think I didn’t hear what you said about me. It’s rude to talk badly about people behind their backs, don’t you know?”

Phainon felt the soft feathers of one of his chickens brush against his leg. Mydeimos must have opened the door to the coop. 

“Thanks for your help,” he said sarcastically, “but I don’t think I’ll be needing it anymore.” He leaned down to pet one of the birds on the head. “We’ll do just fine without your constant negativity.” 

Phainon had always thought himself a people person; he was good at turning conversations in his favor, had a talent at appeasing others with his words. But in this situation, he found himself speechless and dumbfounded. “Understood,” he managed to say.

“And for the record, those cauliflower you said were painfully average ? Aglaea paid premium for them.” 

“I’m…glad.” 

“I’m sure you are.” Mydeimos said with a tight-lipped, obviously insincere smile. 

***

For as long as he could remember, the wheat fields had always been Phainon’s safe escape. 

When he’d gotten into an argument with his sister? He’d retreat to the waves of gold, immersing himself in the scent of grass. If he’d failed a test in school? The gentle breeze and sound of birds singing was a great place to reread those chapters he didn’t understand. 

But no matter what reason he had for coming here, he always tended to do this-to fall asleep, and wake up an hour later with stray strands of straw in his hair and an open book toppled over onto the ground.

Sometimes he’d panic, checking to see if the pages of the book he dropped had dirt stains on them. Other times-like now-he’d be answering to the passerby who found him passed out among the wheat. 

“Is there a reason you’re sleeping out here?” Castorice asked, looking down at him. 

“Not really,” Phainon said sheepishly. “It just happened. By accident.” 

“Well, you may want to stand up.” Castorice leaned down to pick up the novel Phainon had been reading off the ground, scanning the exposed pages for any damage. “The summer is quickly approaching. Who knows? There may be some early-arrival mosquitoes hanging about.”

”Don’t even put that idea out into the world,” Phainon grumbled.  

“You’re lucky that mosquitoes are going to be your only concern within the coming week,” she said. “Crop farmers are going to have a lot of work to do.” 

She was right. The turning of the seasons were some of the busiest times in the Valley-as busy as it could get in a town with a population of 20, anyway. For a rancher like Phainon, the transition from Spring to Summer was hardly trouble at all. But when their plants went out of season, farmers would be going in and out of town to Aglaea’s shop, blueberry and melon seeds in hand. 

Aglaea’s…plants…Phainon threw his head in his hands, resisting the urge to scream. 

“Phainon? Are you okay?” 

“Yeah. I’m doing fine. Perfect, actually. Just peachy.” 

“With every word you say, you sound more distressed.” 

“I’m okay, honest!” Phainon insisted. “Just…came to a sudden realization.”

He’d come to the wheat fields-his beloved, calm, pool of gold-to forget about his stupid encounter with Mydeimos that morning. The realization that he’d be seeing him run in and out of town the next few days was not what he wanted to awaken to. 

“That?” 

That the “city slicker” Phainon had been thinking badly of since his arrival in the Valley would be the General Goods Store’s biggest customer. That he’d run into the man he’d had a confrontation with that very morning, and feel so very small when their eyes locked. That a part of him regretted his actions the past month, but he couldn’t take any of it back. 

“I won’t bore you with all the details,” Phainon said. It was an excuse, clear as day-he knew Castorice would scold him, and he wasn’t awake enough to take it yet. “Let’s just say I’ve dug myself into this hole.” 

“I see,” she said. “Well, that’s not unusual for you.” 

“What-hey!” 

“May this serve as a lesson for you-both on not prematurely passing judgment and learning how to whisper.” She cut Phainon off, who was already beginning to speak. “Yes, I know exactly what you’re talking about.”

Phainon chuckled nervously. “Am I really that terrible at controlling my facial expressions?”

“Yes,” she said bluntly, and handed Phainon’s book back to him. “Page 134 is crinkled. You’d best hope Anaxa doesn’t notice it was you.” 

He took the book back, and flipped to the page. “Cas,” he mumbled, the wrinkled paper staring back at him, “why does it feel like the universe is out to get me?” 

“You already told me that you did this to yourself, so I won’t make you listen to it a second time,” she told him. 

”I don’t know,” Phainon mumbled. “I didn’t think I was wrong in my initial assessment of him. But hearing him talk today? He seemed genuinely hurt.”

”That’s all it took for you to change your attitude? One conversation?” 

“I don’t know,” Phainon said. “Stupid city boys. I gave him genuine, constructive criticism, and he took it personally. I guess they’re sensitive over there.” 

The truth was, if Mydeimos had said the same things to Phainon, Cyrene would have had to hold him back. He was deflecting, and he knew he was; Castorice did too, if the way she was glaring at him was any indication.

“I hope that you’re purposefully acting obtuse,” she said. “Because otherwise, you spent half your day getting eaten alive by mosquitoes for no reason.” 

“Wha-summer doesn’t start for another five days!” 

“My appointment with Tribios is soon,” Castorice said, ignoring him. He scowled as he felt what he hoped was a ghost of an itch on his ankle. 

“Yeah, yeah. Have fun.” 

Tribios was the town’s resident witch. She lived in the outskirts of Cindersap Forest-an elusive figure who few had the opportunity to speak to. In Phainon’s encounters with her, he’d found her-and her Chimeras-good company. He’d for sure be asking Castorice what their appointment was about tomorrow, especially now that his daily schedule had an open slot. 

He picked hay strands out of his hair, guilt gnawing at him as the morning’s events replayed in his head once again. 

If he looked at it objectively-no bias-Mydeimos had done nothing wrong. Sure he’d beaten Phainon at his own tradition, grumbled about the formalities, had a stare that made Phainon feel so so small, and sounded overly polite at times…but if Castorice had told him she disliked someone for those reasons, he’d think her petty. 

Was he really such a sore loser-an accusation from Cyrene he’d defended himself against for years? Or was his intuition right, and the bad vibe he’d gotten from Mydeimos on their first meeting was for good reason? 

Phainon yelped when he felt something small land on his leg. He slapped his hand over the bare skin, expecting a springtime mosquito and breathing a sigh of relief when it was only a blade of grass. 

Further ponderings could wait for his bedroom; Castorice’s terrifying comment wouldn’t be leaving Phainon’s brain anytime soon.

chapters.html:
“That’s a good boy.”

Pie-non, Phainon’s favorite sheep, baah’d affectionately as Phainon scratched his head. A heap of soft, white wool rested in the basket he was carrying; he would be taking it to Aglaea’s today. She loved Kaslanan wool. She told him every time he stopped by. 

The sun’s rays ruthlessly bore down in the Valley. Phainon was sure Pie-non was grateful for being sheared. If the heat was difficult for him to withstand, he couldn’t imagine what it would feel like with a thick layer of wool.

Baah!

“What’s the matter, boy?” 

"It’s just me.” Cyrene stepped into the barn. “Wool all sheared?” 

Phainon handed the basket over. “Pie-non’s finest,” he said with a proud smile. 

“Are you ever going to stop calling him that?” 

“Not unless Cipher gives him a better one next time she comes back.” 

Pie-non had gotten his name from an old friend of Phainon’s. Cipher had grown up alongside him in the Valley, but the small town life didn’t suit her as much as it suited him. She left when she turned 18, and while she did come back from time to time, she spent most of her time on the road; Phainon would get postcards from her, the scenic photographs tacked to his wall. 

The sheep’s name may be a silly way to commemorate someone, but coming up with a new one at this stage seemed wrong. In any case, Pie-non responded to it now. 

“As long as he likes it, I suppose.” Cyrene said with a smile, her fingers brushing over his wool. “You were right about it being his finest, Phainon. Aglaea’s going to love this. I’ll take it down to her shop right now.”

“Right now?” Phainon asked. 

“In case you forgot, it’s Tuesday.” She smiled. “It’ll be a good change of pace for me. Go do something you enjoy, lil bro.” 

“Why do you keep calling me that? ” 

***

Phainon completed his morning chores within the hour. A shower, hair dry and change of clothes later, he found himself on his way to the old Community Center. 

To most of the town, the Community Center was abandoned. The outside was littered with overgrown plants, the windows broken and eerie. Children whispered that it was haunted. Krateros assured them that the footsteps they claimed to hear was just their imagination, but Phainon knew better. The light pattering belonged to the Chimeras.

Very few people knew about the furry, cat-like creatures, and even fewer were able to communicate with them. Phainon had learned quickly to keep his gift a secret; not only did the Chimeras not like attracting attention to themselves, but anyone Phainon told only seemed jealous of his ability. He took no joy in seeing Cipher and Castorice feel excluded, and if he needed to, he knew Anaxa and Cyrene also shared his talent. 

Phainon felt the small clump of Pie-non’s wool in his pocket. He often took goods from the Ranch as presents for the creatures, and while she hadn’t said anything, he knew Cyrene noticed. If she wasn’t friends with the Chimeras too, he was sure he would’ve had his ear talked off by now.

He walked through the entrance; he felt the wooden floorboards below him waver, the creaking noise no doubt signaling the Chimeras of his arrival. Sure enough, it only took a few seconds for those footsteps to sound, and…

”…Phainon?” 

Phainon almost jumped out of his skin. “Mydeimos!” He squeaked. “What…what are you doing in here?” 

As if to answer his question, an orange-furred creature walked between Mydeimos’ legs. He mewled as he nuzzled against his ankle, obviously familiar with the new farmer.

”You…can see the Chimeras?” Phainon asked. 

“Yes?” Mydeimos knelt down, putting himself on petting level with the Chimera. “What, is that unusual?” 

“Well, yeah!” Phainon exclaimed, before noticing the sour look on Mydeimos’ face. “I mean, not because of where you’re from. It’s just that the Chimeras rarely show themselves, even to people who’ve lived here their entire lives-so I guess maybe it is, but not in a bad way-“

The Chimera yowled loudly, cutting Phainon off mid-sentence. He silently thanked the small creature for saving him from further embarrassment. 

“Interesting,” Mydeimos mused. “These little guys showed themselves to me a week after I moved in. Guess my old life in the city isn’t as unforgivable as some think.”

Phainon’s mouth gaped open. The combination of learning the Chimeras had shown themselves to Mydeimos within seven days and his not-so-subtle dig at Phainon made him forget all about the wool in his pocket. “Look, I’m sorry about what I said to you. And about you.” 

Mydeimos raised an eyebrow. “So the Chimeras’ seal of approval was what you needed to accept me into your perfect little town?” 

He winced. “No, I…it’s been on my mind for a while. The idea of apologizing, that is.” 

“…Are your apologies always so…” Mydeimos trailed off. “What’s the word? Messy?” 

“No! I’m perfectly capable of giving a thought-out and heartfelt apology! It’s not like I knew I would be seeing you here today!”

Phainon heard the Chimera’s pleased purr when Mydeimos scratched their ears. “Well, we’re both here now,” he said, petting the fuzzy animal. “And I have time. Come on. Think up your most convincing apology.” 

“Now?” Phainon asked. “On the spot?”

“Backing away from a challenge so easily?” Mydeimos taunted. “And here I was, thinking you’d be more…adaptable than this.” 

“I’m not backing away! ” Phainon bristled. Mydeimos only stared back at him without saying a word. He was waiting for that apology, and Phainon knew it.

“Okay, okay…I’m sorry for insulting your crops. And for accusing you of not cleaning up after your chickens. And for making fun of you for being Okheman. And for calling your porch decorations ugly. And for telling my sister you cheated at the Egg Hunt.”

“Do you want to add anything else?” Phainon could be mistaken, but he thought Mydeimos sounded… amused?

“I’m also sorry for calling the color you painted your coop tacky.”

Neither of them spoke for several minutes. The only noise came from the birds outside and the Chimeras prowling about-including the frustrated growl from the orange one by Mydeimos’ side, who he had stopped petting while lost in thought.

“Here’s my review,” he said finally. “I don’t think your tone sounds too sorry, but I appreciate how you outright laid everything out. Humiliating yourself to show your sincerity is an interesting tactic. Overall, I’ll give it a 6.5/10.”

“Wha-that’s not even a passing grade! What do I have to do to get that last 4%?” 

The Chimera shoved their head into Mydeimos’ hand before he started stroking their fur again. “Prove yourself through your actions instead of your words.”

“Does this mean you want me to help you on the farm again?” He wasn’t sure why the prospect excited him; he still wasn’t very fond of the other man, yet he found himself wanting a second chance. A fresh start.

”No. You don’t get to come back onto my land until you get to 70%.” 

“Then how am I supposed to…wait, what do you mean, 70%? A passing grade is a 69%!” 

“We’re high achievers in the city,” Mydeimos said, a smirk forming on his face. Did he enjoy riling Phainon up like this? 

“I-whatever! I don’t even know why I want your approval anyway!” 

Phainon may have stormed out right then and there, but saw a blur of blue fur dashing toward him. Bubbles-one of the Chimeras-purred as he nuzzled against Phainon’s bare legs, soft fur touching his skin. 

“Hey little guy!” Phainon said, kneeling down to pet him. While he was fond of all the Chimeras, he was the closest with Bubbles. They’d been exchanging gifts since Phainon was a kid; the young boy would bring ranch products, and the Chimera would present little knickknacks he came across. Phainon never visited the Community Center without a treat for his companion. “Don’t worry buddy. I got a treat for you, as always.” 

“Seems that blue one really likes you,” Mydeimos commented, watching where Bubbles’ tail was hitting Phainon’s lower leg. He mewled excitedly when he saw Pie-non’s wool, raising himself up onto his hind legs to take it in his mouth. 

“Name’s Bubbles,” Phainon said, scratching him on the head before he scampered away. “It’s a routine we have. I give him something from the farm, and he’ll gift me something he’s found in this place.” 

As if on queue, the little animal came back with what looked like a gemstone in its small mouth. He dropped it at Phainon’s feet, looking up at him with a proud expression on his face. “Let’s see,” Phainon said softly. 

“That’s a Tigerseye,” Mydeimos said. He was looking at the stone, and Phainon couldn’t help but notice his eyes matched its color. “I just donated one to the museum a while ago. I wonder where he got his paws on one of those.” 

Phainon furrowed his brows. “Where did you get one of those?” 

“The Mines,” he said simply, as if that explained everything. “They’re pretty rare, actually.”

He traced his thumbpad over the orange surface of the stone, feeling the rough texture on his skin. “It’s beautiful,” he said, and Bubbles purred satisfactorily. “Thank you, friend.” 

“D’you think he knows the value of that gem?” 

“Not sure,” Phainon said truthfully. “But I’m more interested in the fact that you’ve apparently been cave spelunking .”

“I have,” Mydeimos said. He rose to his feet, causing the Chimera to whine in protest. “It’s getting late, little one. I gotta head back, alright?” 

“Are you going to elaborate on that at all, or just leave me hanging?” 

“You’ll unlock the story privileges once you get that passing grade.” The two walked out of the Community Center together; Mydeimos was right, it was getting late. Phainon saw the familiar glowing of lightning bugs, and had to resist the urge to catch one in his palms. 

“Do you see these in Okhema, too?” Phainon asked. 

“Fireflies, you mean? “Yes, but not in abundance like this.” Mydeimos stopped walking, and Phainon watched as the lights flickered around them. “Beautiful, aren’t they?”

“Yeah, they are.” Phainon said, then turned to face him. “Hey, wanna see me catch one?” 

“Who are we? Children?” 

“We?” Phainon asked. “What, do you wanna compete? See who can catch one first?” 

Mydeimos looked at him. “…How do you make sure you don’t kill them?” 

“What? City boy never caught a lightning bug before?” He smiled wide. “Afraid of hurting them too, hm? Looks like Mydeimos over here is a real softie.” 

“Shut up,” he grumbled. “Whatever. I’ll watch you catch one first.”

“Alright,” Phainon said, grinning from ear to ear. “Watch how a professional does it.” 

With a look back to see if Mydeimos was watching, Phainon looked for a bug within arms’ reach. His tongue poked out slightly as he focused, his hands cupped. When he got close enough, he reached out and clapped them together. “Caught one,” he said, smiling at the yellow light shining between his fingers. 

“So our contest starts now?” Mydeimos asked. His eyes followed the lightning bug that Phainon just released. 

“On the count of three,” he replied. “I’ll even give you a five second head start.”

“Be careful with that overconfidence, Phainon . Remember what happened the last time?” 

“Don’t you worry. I won’t make the same mistake twice.”

As it turned out, Phainon was right. Even with a several extra seconds, Mydeimos still came out on bottom. He stared at his opponents’ glowing, cupped hands with disbelief. “You make it look so easy.” 

“You just gotta commit,” he said nonchalantly, opening his hands and letting the insect fly away. “You almost had one, but you hesitated.”

”Don’t you know fireflies are threatened nowadays?” Mydeimos protested. “I’m not going to make myself talk of the town by killing your protected wildlife.” 

Phainon smiled. “Like I said. You look tough, but it turns out that you’re a total softie.” 

“It’s late,” Mydeimos said, ignoring Phainon’s comment. “I’ll be heading back now. Goodnight.”

“Goodnight to you too." Phainon watched the farmer's retreating back, framed by the glow of the streetlamps and starlight.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Summer 13, Year 1
chapters.html:
“What time does the Saloon open again?” 

Phainon and Castorice were sitting on the beach pier, Cipher between them. Her visit was a surprise; she’d shown up at the bus stop at 1pm, and neither of them knew until she sent them a text telling them she had arrived. 

“It’s technically open now,” Castorice told her. “But nobody will be there but the staff. It really only gets busy around 6.” 

Cipher swung her legs back and forth. She’d cut her hair shorter since they’d last met, but otherwise she looked the same as Phainon remembered: silver locks, prominent fangs, and two pointy ears and a tail. He was surpris ed she agreed to go to the dock. His catlike friend had always disliked water, and the large fish in the ocean often splashed small waves onto the people sitting by.

“About an hour and a half then,” Cipher said, looking at her watch. “Eugh. You know I love you guys, but living here is so boring . I don’t know how I did it for so many years.”

”If you tell us you’re coming next time, we could plan something to do,” Castorice said. 

“I don’t know,” she said, stretching her arms behind her with a yawn. “Life’s best lived spontaneously.”

Phainon had heard plenty of Cipher’s “spur of the moment” stories. Her eyes glowed when she reflected on stepping into shady clubs or hooking up with strangers, and while he never judged her, Phainon didn’t understand the appeal. “Guess we really are country bumpkins, aren’t we Cas?” He joked.

“You more so than me. You’ve never even left the Valley.” 

“Yes I have!”

”Let me rephrase that. You haven’t left the Valley within the past fifteen years.” 

Phainon said nothing to that, and only glared. Cipher snorted. “Alright, alright. If you guys do the planning, we can schedule a trip where all three of us go to Okhema. I know all the best spots.”

“Like…?” 

“Restaurants, outdoor concert venues, the like,” she said. “Don’t worry. I won’t be traumatizing our dear Phainon by dragging him into a club.  The smell of weed will be scandalous enough for him.”

“That’s our Cipher,” Castorice said sarcastically. “Always so thoughtful and compassionate.” 

“You’re too kind.” The silver-haired girl scooted away from the edge of the pier to stand up. “What would you all say about walking around a bit before heading to the bar?”

“Sure,” Castorice said. “It’s been a while since you’ve come back and seen the town.”

“You make it sound like things have changed since then.” 

A few complaints about the sand later, the group left the beach. “Where do you wanna walk? We can go anywhere but the museum.” 

“Awwh, why not?” Cipher whined. “Those nice, shiny, gems are the most appealing part of this town.” 

“Please. Phainon and I both remember what happened the last time we let you near that place.”

Several years have passed since Castorice and Phainon had made the fatal mistake of leading Cipher around the library and museum. She’d slipped a ruby from the display case into her pocket; it was only at the bus stop when Cipher was about to leave that Phainon noticed the red gleam. 

He suspected it was on purpose. A thief as skilled as her would never make a mistake like that. Still, it was best to avoid conflict with Anaxa.

“Oh come on, Cas. That was years ago.” Cipher huffed. “And you got it back in the end, didn’t you? I don’t see what the big deal is-hold on. Who’s that?” 

“Who?” Castorice asked. 

“Walking toward the Saloon. Blond hair.” She cocked her head. “Wow. Did someone new move into Pelican Town?” 

Phainon’s eyes drifted to the Saloon, where Mydeimos was swinging the door open and stepping inside. The two hadn’t spoken more than a few casual words in passing since the day at the Community Center. While Phainon felt as if they parted on good terms, the thought of seeing him again made him nervous.

“Oh, Mydeimos? He moved in at the beginning of this year.”

“And what’s with you, Phainon? You’ve been staring at that door since he walked through it.” 

Phainon tore his eyes away from the Saloon. “Nothing,” he said quickly.

“He and Mydeimos have some…unresolved problems,” Castorice said. 

“Phainon? Making enemies?” Cipher whistled. “What happened to the boy scout I grew up with?” 

“We’re not enemies,” Phainon said. “We’re even on amicable terms now. I told you this already, Cas.”

The day after their night with the Chimeras, Phainon had dropped by Castorice’s house and told her everything. She’d listened attentively, picking up every detail, even adding in her own comments- seems to me like he wants to be friends with you, Phainon, considering he accepted that shoddy apology. 

I don’t-what do you mean shoddy apology? I tried my hardest!  

“Not enemies? Then what’s the unresolved tension about? Don’t tell me…did our sweet Phainon finally get laid?” 

“Huh? No!” Phainon spluttered, eyes widened in shock. “What gave you that idea?” 

“Sorry, sorry,” she said, though Phainon thought that she sounded especially unapologetic. He glared at her.

“We were…unfriendly with each other from the start, but we’ve since made amends. It’s still…just a bit awkward.” 

Phainon had thought about his conversation with Castorice more often than he’d like to admit. He wasn’t sure why he wanted Mydeimos to like him, or why Mydeimos would even want to be his friend. 

Think about it. You’re guys of similar age, similar age, with a similar competitive spirit. It makes sense to me. 

I don’t know, Cas. It seemed to me like he thought my “competitive spirit” was a character flaw.

“Well, it seems like people are coming in early,” Castorice said. “We can go now, if you want to.”

“Lead the way.”

***

Cipher leaned forward as she aimed her pool stick. The tip of the cue hit one of the colorful balls, scattering several of Phainon’s into the holes on the side. “Shame,” she said. “And here I was thinking you would’ve improved over the years.” 

“I have improved!” Phainon said defensively. “I just had a bad start this round.” 

“Mhm. And what about the last game with Castorice? You actually had a pretty good lead at the beginning.” 

“We almost tied. You can’t hold that against me-wait, where did you get that candy bar? I thought you said you didn’t have any money on you.”

”I don’t,” Cipher said, taking another bite of her chocolate bar. 

Castorice snorted. “You best hope Cerydra doesn’t notice you did that,” she said. 

“Oh please. I’ve been doing this for years. Haven’t been caught once. It’s your turn, Phainon, by the way.” 

“Right,” he said, picking up his cue. “Sorry.” 

As much as he loathed to admit it, Phainon was severely distracted. It wasn’t unusual for him to lose to Cipher at pool-it was normal, actually-but this badly? He tried his best to concentrate, to aim well and ignore Mydeimos’ conversation with Cerydra behind him. 

“If you’re interested, Cas, I could teach you.” Cipher said. “Or I can just grab another one.” 

“I’m okay, thank you.”

Mydeimos and Cerydra were discussing what sounded like selling milk; he must be treating his new cows well. It had only been a week since Cyrene had given the calves a new home, and they were already producing milk worthy of the Stardrop Saloon. 

“Phainon, you missed entirely again,” Castorice said. He jumped, startled-he was completely lost in thought again.

”Ah,” he said simply, looking at the state of the table. 

“What’s got you so distracted?” Cipher finished off the last of the chocolate, stuffing the wrapper in her pocket. “Is it Mr. Eye Candy back there?” 

When the three of them entered the Saloon, the first thing Cipher did was look at the Valley’s new arrival. After about a solid minute of obvious staring, Mydeimos had walked up to them and asked Cipher what she needed. The introduction between the two of them was one of the most awkward moments Phainon had ever witnessed. It didn’t stop her from commenting on his appearance when he was out of earshot, though. He’s a pretty one, isn’t he? 

“He’s the new owner of my cows,” Phainon huffed. “Of course I’m interested in hearing about how they’re doing.” 

Cipher positioned her cue with pristine precision. With one strike, she brought the game to an end. “You’ve been selling cows your whole life, farm boy,” she said. “What I’m interested in is how special these cows are. They must be, right? If they caused the game to be thrown this badly.” 

“Can I not care about the wellbeing of my animals?” 

Cipher sighed, and leaned down to pick the pool rack off the ground. “Stop dodging the question. You know what I meant. Castorice, are you sure he’s not hiding something from us?” 

“If he was, he would’ve spilled it to me by now,” she said. “He can’t keep a secret for the world.”

Phainon said nothing. He couldn’t argue with that. 

“Shit,” Cipher suddenly whispered, looking behind them. “Stop talking. Both of you.” 

Curious to know what made Cipher go quiet, Phainon turned around to look where Cipher’s eyes were; he went stiff when he saw the subject of their conversation. 

“My apologies,” Mydeimos said. His voice was rich and warm; clearer in Phainon’s ears than when he’d been eavesdropping earlier in the evening. “I hope I’m not interrupting anything. I just think I left something of mine over here…”

“Don’t apologize. We actually just finished up our game. Feel free to look around all you want!” 

Phainon saw Cipher put a hand to her mouth, poorly concealing laughter. He shot her a glare. 

“No need,” he said, bending down to pick up a water bottle off the ground. “I’ll be heading home now. See you around.”

He gave a small smile-a soft and gentle expression-and Phainon felt his heartrate spike. “Yeah,” he said, hoping the smile was for him. 

***

It wasn’t until closing time that Cipher, Castorice, and Phainon left the Saloon. The night was pitch dark, the only light coming from the streetlamps and the moon.

”Well, I was originally planning on taking the bus back home,” Cipher said. “But it seems I’ve missed it by a few hours.” 

”Ah,” Castorice said. “I’m sorry. I should’ve kept track of time better.” 

“Oh, Cas. I never said I was complaining!” She smiled gleefully. “The more time I spend here, the more time I get to hear about our Deliverer’s little crush. ” 

“You won’t be hearing anything,” Phainon said. “Because I don’t have one. Why do you want me to so badly?” 

“Isn’t the mental gymnastics of trying to explain why you blush whenever that guy looks at you exhausting? It’ll be so relieving to just admit it.”

“I already explained that to you. It’s because we got off to a bad start. Any sign that he doesn’t dislike me anymore is going to make me feel better.”

”And why do you want him to like you so badly?”

Phainon stopped walking. “…I’m not sure.”

She snorted. “God, you’re unbelievable.” 

Ever since Mydeimos had left the building, Phainon had the feeling the walk back would be like this. He’d thought up pre-prepared answers in his head while Cipher and Castorice talked over drinks, tricking himself into believing he would survive her questioning with ease. Yet, it felt like she was ripping into him; she’d always been playful and a fan of teasing, but this felt more…personal.

He saw Castorice give him a sympathetic smile. His discomfort must be written all over his face. As usual.

“Well, in any case, here we are,” Cipher said, standing in front of the ranch. “We’ll see you tomorrow morning, then? 10am?”

“Yeah,” Phainon said absentmindedly. He was already thinking about the comfort of his bed. “Goodnight, both of you.”

Chapter End Notes

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Summer 28, Year 1
chapters.html:
The sky was always clear on the last day of Summer. 

This was regarded as a blessing from most of the Valley; some said that it was a gift from the Chimeras, keeping the weather nice for the Dance of the Moonlight Jellies. As much as Phainon loved seeing the jellyfish, he would be the first to admit the sunny weather in the hottest month of the year made for miserable working conditions. 

He set his hoe down, lifting his shirt to wipe a pool of sweat off his forehead. Fall was the prime season for growing Amaranth, his cows’ favorite treat. He and Cyrene had a pitiful harvest the year before, and Phainon had been waiting for a chance to redeem the Kaslana Ranch since; he’d be damned if he let some heat stop him.

“Hey, you want some help?” 

Phainon jumped, the hem of his now sweat-soaked shirt falling back down. “Mydeimos,” he said, voice wavering. “How…how long have you been standing there?” 

“Not long.” Mydeimos had his hair tied back today, presumably to keep it out of his face while doing farm work. It suited him. “Just enough to see you pulling out dead crops.” 

“…The goats enjoy dead hay more. It was on purpose.”

Mydeimos snorted. “Right. So, is that a yes or a no on the help?” 

“What’s in it for you? Don’t you have work to do on your own land?” 

“What’s in it for me is being able to buy quality food for my livestock. And I’ve done everything I can for the day. The rest can’t be worked on until tomorrow.” 

“Oh, yeah.” Unlike Phainon and Cyrene, who’d lived in the Valley for over two decades, Mydeimos hadn’t been able to stockpile Fall seeds from years before. “Well, if you insist…” 

Mydeimos put his hands on the wooden fence, hoisting himself to the top. Phainon heard a faint creak and winced; he’d just replaced the barrier the year prior, and wasn’t enjoying the idea of rebuilding it. “Careful with that fence, please.” 

Phainon’s new guest lowered himself, landing on the Rancher’s side of the fence. “Really? It can handle a 1,000 pound cow, but I’m too heavy?” 

“The cows typically don’t put their whole weight on it,” Phainon grumbled. “Whatever. Are you going to help like you said you would, or did you just want to break my fence?” 

“Who do you take me for? Just tell me what you want me to do.” 

***

Phainon wasn’t sure what made him say yes to Mydeimos’ proposal. It had only been a season since he was mocking his Okheman background, convinced he wouldn’t be able to lift a shovel. But if Phainon hadn’t been proven wrong by Mydeimos’ financial success in the Valley, he would’ve been by seeing him in action. 

The man made the farmwork look easy; he effortlessly tilled the earth, back muscles rippling through his dampened shirt. At least that’s what Phainon thought he saw. He noticed sweat glistening on the back of his exposed neck, heard his heavier breathing through the labor. If Phainon had been beheld to this sight beforehand, he never would have believed Mydeimos came from the city.

“Tell me about this Amaranth,” Mydeimos said suddenly. Breathily . It snapped Phainon out of his thoughts, making him jump.

“We plant it for our cows. They go crazy for it.” 

“Hm. How long do they take to grow?” 

“A week, exactly. They’re not that profitable, if that’s why you’re asking. Just cow treats. You’d be better off just buying a couple.” 

“Asking me to buy from you? Are you sure this isn’t just a sales pitch?” 

Mydeimos turned around then-and with his sweat stricken, dirt-stained face- smiled . Phainon froze in place, feeling his heart skip several beats. “Um,” he said dumbly, eyes fixed on the man in front of him. “I mean…if it means you’ll come back more often, feel free…?” 

“Are these the kind of lines you country folk use?” Mydeimos laughed. 

“Lines?” Phainon repeated faintly. His mind was anywhere but their current conversation-he was replaying Mydeimos’ laugh over and over again in his head. He never would have guessed that his nature could be so… gentle . 

“You know what? Never mind.” 

Mydeimos propped the hoe against the side of the barn; Phainon watched him wordlessly, debating whether or not to press him further on what he meant. Before he could make a decision, though, Mydeimos announced his leave. 

“I’ll see you tonight at the Dance of the Moonlight Jellies?” Mydeimos asked, walking toward the fence gate. 

“Oh! That’s right! It’ll be your first time seeing it, won’t it?” Phainon said cheerfully. He dashed toward the wooden gate, unclasping the lock to let Mydeimos through. “I’ll definitely be there. There hasn’t been a year where I’ve missed it.” 

“Glad to hear it. I’ll be looking for you.”

He’ll be looking for him. For some reason, the words made Phainon feel giddy.

“I’m looking forward to it.”

***

“Wait. Did you just call them Lunaloos?” 

Phainon was sitting on the dock, Mydeimos and Castorice on either side. The three of them had arrived a little early; there was about half an hour until the jellyfish were due to appear, and Castorice had taken it upon herself to teach their Okheman friend about the species.

”Did you really think their scientific name was Moonlight Jellies?” 

“I’d argue Lunaloos sounds even less like a scientific name.” 

Phainon swung his legs back and forth over the ocean, listening to two of them banter back and forth with a stupid smile on his face. Mydeimos put on a serious front in the presence of most people, but Phainon preferred him like this; unfiltered and unguarded, speaking amongst friends between laughter. 

Castorice let out an exaggerated sigh. “Phainon. What do you think sounds more official?” 

“Moonlight Jellies.” His answer was instantaneous, without hesitation.

“See? Even he agrees with me.” 

“What do you mean, even me? ” Phainon expressed indignantly. 

“I wouldn’t take it too seriously. He’s been looking for chances to get on your good side,” Castorice said. Phainon shot her a dirty look.

“Oh, I see . You’re just ganging up on me.”

Mydeimos laughed; it was something he’d been doing a lot lately, but it always affected Phainon like it was the first time. It seemed to be contagious this time, too, if the smile creeping onto Phainon’s face was any indication. 

“You say that, but you’re smiling.”

“Shut up, Cas. You’re lucky we’re next to the ocean. Otherwise, I’d tackle Mydeimos right here and now.”

”Careful. You’re only a few points away from that 70%. You wouldn’t want to get knocked back down, would you?” 

Phainon sighed dramatically. “And now I’m being threatened. Whatever will I do?” 

He wasn’t sure where his confidence had come from, and for a moment, was worried he’d overestimated his closeness with Mydeimos. The last thing he wanted was to undo all the progress they’d made over the Summer. But Mydeimos just gave an, “oh I wonder,” smile never leaving his face. 

“Look!” Phainon heard one of the village Children, Livia, shout. “Here they come!” 

The waters quickly lit up as the jellyfish showed off their glow. One by one, they drifted away from the Valley, starting their annual migration to a warmer climate. Phainon experienced this every year-feeling the last of warm Summer air and hearing the cicadas chirp while the lights in the sea grew smaller and smaller. No matter how many times he watched, it never became less beautiful. 

He heard a sharp intake of breath next to him. Phainon looked to his right, where Mydeimos was watching the Jellies with adept attention. His eyes, locked onto the fishes’ dance, seemed to be sparkling; his mouth slightly agape as white light emerged from the water. He looked as though he was witnessing magic, which Phainon could only assume this must be like for him-such mesmerizing displays could only be seen in animals’ natural environments, away from cities like Okhema.

“They’re beautiful ,” he said. 

The Summer Night sky was dark, and the only illumination came from the jellyfish and the Fisherman’s Shop’s flickering outdoor lights. Phainon didn’t know when his focus had shifted from the Moonlight Jellies’ Dance, but he noticed in the faint glow how pretty Mydeimos’ eyelashes were; he watched the other man aptly as he marveled at the spectacle, smiling at his enthusiasm and awe. 

“Aren’t they?” Phainon breathed out, his blue eyes still fixated on Mydeimos. 

“I’ve never seen anything like it.” 

Phainon wasn’t sure if Cipher meant what she’d said to him a couple weeks back; it wasn’t unlike her to say things for the sake of teasing. But it had been on his mind nonetheless- The Deliverer’s little crush. Phainon knew the way he felt around Mydeimos versus his other friends was different, but didn’t think that a crush was the right word for it. Until now. 

Until he set his eyes on Mydeimos’ softly parted lips, heard his heartbeat pounding in his ears. Until the last jellyfish disappeared from the visible waters, and Mydeimos still hadn’t torn his gaze away from the ocean. Until he felt Castorice hit him on the shoulder, and he’d turned around to a satisfied and knowing smirk on her face. 

If it weren’t for the entire population of the Valley being gathered at the pier, Phainon would’ve screamed. It didn’t make sense; he’d hated the guy a month ago! Where did this come from? 

The revelation made him feel like running away. Maybe if he avoided Mydeimos, the feelings would dissipate. They could be nothing more than friends, their relationship akin to his with Castorice or Cipher.

But fuck , he thought, listening to Mydeimos gush about the Dance. He spoke of how enchanting the jellyfish were in the water, how fascinating the aquatic creatures were, how amazing it was to see them in their natural habitat. There was no kidding himself. To be nothing more than friends wasn’t what he wanted. 

He turned to Castorice, who was still smiling slyly at him. Cas , he mouthed, the desperation present even through lip reading. What am I going to do?

chapters.html:
“Long time, no see!”

It took seconds after Phainon and Castorice got off the bus for Cipher to run up to them. “It hasn’t even been a month,” Castorice said, Cipher hugging her. 

“It felt longer,” Cipher said, letting go of the girl to give Phainon a hug too. “How’s life on the farm, Rancher Boy?” 

“I have some choice words for you.” 

Cipher pulled back with raised eyebrows. “Ouch. What made you so upset?” 

Phainon sighed, sharing a look with Castorice. “Let’s talk as we walk,” he said. 

To Cipher’s credit, she really was familiar with Okhema’s best spots. She took them along the bustling streets, leading them to the city’s center park. It was different from home; the grass was unnaturally green, and the lake fountains were artificial, but it beat the other options for scenery. 

“You didn’t speak while we walked here, so you will now,” Cipher said, as the three of them sat down on a bench. “Even if you didn’t let it slip when you got here, it’s clear something’s on your mind. Let it out.” 

Phainon stared at the water splashing from the fountains. “You were right,” he said quietly. “Or you planted that stupid idea into my head. One or the other.” 

Cipher cocked her head. “Stop beating around the bush. Say what you mean.” 

Phainon glared at her. She knew exactly what he was referring to; she just wanted to make him say it out loud. “You’re smart. Figure it out for yourself.”

“Remember the new boy in town? The one you said Phainon was into?” Castorice interjected. “I had the pleasure of listening to him talk about the guy every day for the past week.”

“Cas, please,” Phainon said, voice pained. “That’s enough .” 

The day after the Dance of the Moonlight Jellies, Phainon had come over to Castorice’s house to play video games. Halfway through their first round of Journey to the Prairie King, he broke down and spilled everything; he recounted how Mydeimos helped him on the farm the previous morning, then described how effortlessly gorgeous he looked that night.

Fuck ,  Phainon had sworn. His eyelashes are so pretty. How have I never noticed them before?

Ew. Cut it out. Castorice complained, though she smiled.

“You think it’s fair to gush about him to me for several hours and make me keep it to myself? I deserve some compensation.” 

“You’re lucky there’s so many people around,” he grumbled. “Otherwise, I would strangle you. ” 

“So you really do have a crush on him then,” Cipher mused. “Tell me about him.” 

“Careful. I’m not sure you know what you’re asking for.”

Phainon rolled his eyes. “You already know all you need to know. He’s the new farmer who moved in from Okhema. Stop trying to embarrass me.”

“You don’t have to worry about that,” Cipher said, looking at him slyly. “You embarrass yourself enough as is.” 

“Oh, that’s really going to make me want to tell you.”

It was quiet for a minute. Phainon shifted his focus back to the lake; there was a group of ducks swimming in the water, dunking their upper bodies in the pond and paddling their little feet. With a wail, Phainon was reminded of Mydeimos again-he had the exact same kind of bird on his farm. 

“Fuck, Cipher, he took off his shirt the other day,” he whined, throwing his head into his hands. The ducks quacked in surprise at the commotion, darting to the other end of the lake. “He’s ripped. I think his tattoos go all the way down to….you know. And I think he saw me staring at him.” 

“Yikes. You’ve got it bad.”

“Tell me about it.” His face was still covered by his hands, muffling his voice. 

“So…what are you planning on doing about it?” 

Phainon moved his hands away. His face was reddened, both from the pressure put on his skin and a furious blush. “I’m waiting for it to pass and pretending it never happened.” 

Cipher stared at him in disbelief. “You expect that to work when you see the guy every day?” 

“I told you, Phainon,” Castorice said. “It won’t be easy to just run from this.” 

“From what you’ve told me, Deliverer, it sounds like he might be into you too,” Cipher told him. “Maybe shoot your shot?”

“No. No way,” Phainon said, almost automatically. “Are you serious? I have no idea how to ask someone on a date!” 

“So dramatic.” Cipher rolled her eyes. “It’s not hard. All you have to do is go up to them-“

“I think you’re forgetting that we live in a town with a population with less than two dozen people,” Phainon said, cutting her off. “If it doesn’t go how I want it to, it’ll make both our lives painfully awkward.” 

“Okay, fine. Try thinking about things about the guy you absolutely can’t stand. I’ve done that before, and it’s worked.”

“Like what?” Phainon whined. “The only reason I disliked him at first was because he beat me at the Egg Festival. All that city stuff was just an excuse I made for myself. He’s kind, funny, good with kids, and extremely attractive. There’s nothing to hate about him.” 

Cipher stood up, dragging Phainon with her. “Let’s go for a walk. The concert will be starting in less than two hours. You can give it some thought along the way.”

***

Even though Cipher had told the two of them they’d be in charge of all the planning, she couldn’t resist taking them to one of her favorite local band’s concerts. I go to almost every show at this venue, she’d said in the group chat. They’re the best performers in the area. By far. 

Phainon had never been to a concert-a confession that only fueled Cipher’s desire to drag him and Castorice along. While he had agreed to go, he was still nervous about it; the amount of people that walked past them on the park bench outnumbered his whole town, and the crowd before him now was infinitely bigger.

“I’ve never seen this many people in my entire life,” Phainon said quietly, his eyes wide. “Is it always this crowded?” 

“There’s more people than normal for this time of day,” Cipher told him, “but the show doesn’t start for another hour. I’m guessing that the size of the crowd will double.” 

“Double?” Phainon echoed. “Is it even possible for that many people to fit in here?”

“You should’ve been here a couple years ago.” Phainon and Castorice had to enter a near-run to catch up with Cipher, who had reached a good row on the bleachers. “A local band signed up to perform months prior, but had a song blow up right before their concert. I was standing on the floor, and it felt like I was going to get crushed.”

Phainon stared at the floor, where, currently, a sizable audience had already gathered. “You were down there?” 

“I would be this time too, if you two weren’t with me.” Cipher unzipped her bag to take out a water bottle. “Aren’t I the kindest? Giving up an opportunity to see my favorite band on the floor for my two country bumpkin friends.” 

Castorice began talking to Cipher about something Phainon didn’t understand-girl stuff, probably-so he let himself sit back and breathe. This was the kind of life Mydeimos lived before moving to the Valley; the difference was even starker than Phainon imagined. For him, this trip was a big excursion. For Mydeimos? The throng of people around him now was probably the size of his high school graduating class. 

He’d never asked Mydeimos about his old life in Okhema, but after visiting the place himself, he realized he was curious. He wondered if he knew the city streets like Cipher did, or if he regularly went to shows like these. He wanted to know how Mydeimos adjusted to the Valley; if he missed Okhema, if he longed for that busy life again. 

He saw two women with conjoined take their seats on the bleachers a couple rows ahead of them, prompting another question in Phainon’s head. He scowled. There was no need to ponder on it. Mydeimos had definitely been on a lot of dates. 

Phainon felt that Mydeimos was the forward type. He thought about him going up to a person of interest, asking them out and securing a date like it was the easiest thing in the world. He bristled at the images in his head: Mydeimos paying for a nameless person’s meal at a fancy Okheman restaurant, Mydeimos driving them home in a well-kept car, Mydeimos watching them adoringly as they disappeared inside their abode. 

What Phainon would give to see Mydeimos look at him that way. He could imagine it in his head; the man’s normally sharp gaze that used to make Phainon feel oh-so-small would soften, the bright pools of gold filling with adoration. His soft-looking lips would turn upward into a gentle smile, and he’d bring a calloused hand to cup Phainon’s face. Within their new close proximity Phainon would be able to see those gorgeous eyelashes-the same ones he’d been sneaking glances at since that night the dock.

His eyes would wander down to Mydeimos’ mouth-wonder if his lips felt as nice as they looked, what it would be like if he leaned forward just a little bit and gave himself what he wanted so, so badly. They were so close now- even closer than before, and Phainon would notice that it wasn’t just him-it was Mydeimos pulling them together, Mydeimos causing the rest of the world to fizzle away when his lips met Phainon’s.

How effortlessly it would sweep Phainon away-his kiss would be gentle, testing the waters, but Phainon would drown in it all the same. Mydeimos would smell heavily of soil from hours of farm work, but at their close distance Phainon would pick up the scent of his strawberry shampoo-something he’d only smelled faintly before. He’d move a hand to the back of Mydeimos’ head, let his fingers revel in his soft hair as he started to kiss back.

You’re gorgeous, Phainon would tell him when they parted for air. He’d tuck those stray strands of Mydeimos’ hair that were misplaced by his hand, and oh, the sweet smile on Mydeimos’ face would hit Phainon like a spear to the chest. He’d tilt his head to move back in, hear the crowd scream as-

Hear the crowd scream. Right. He was at a concert, and the band of the hour, Zagreus, just took the stage.  The lead singer-named Bartholos, according to Cipher-announced something that riled the crowd up further, but Phainon didn’t hear what he said. He just stared ahead blankly, processing the daydream he’d just slipped into.

***

“So, what did you think? Do you guys listen to music like that in the boonies?” 

It had been midnight when Zagreus had finished performing, and between weaving through the crowds and stopping at a store along the way, getting to the bus station took an extra hour. Cipher was holding a plastic bag in her hand, a mischievous look on her face. 

“I liked it more than I thought I would,” Castorice admitted, fighting back a yawn. “But I’m too sleepy right now to give a proper review.”

Cipher asked Phainon for his opinion next, to which he mumbled a generic response. While he tried to pay attention to the music, his mind was too occupied with Mydeimos to let anything else in. 

“Before you go,” Cipher purred, “I bought something for you.” She threw the bag at Phainon, who caught it against his chest.

“For me?” Phainon echoed. “Should I…look now?” 

“If you want to.” Contrary to her nonchalant words, Cipher’s expression betrayed that she was very eager for Phainon to see his gift. 

He cautiously looked inside the bag, only to close it immediately. “ No, ” he said quickly. 

“You’d reject my thoughtful gift?” 

“ Cipher, ” Phainon hissed. “You bought me a fleshlight? ” 

He heard Castorice clap a hand over her mouth, the action doing little to hide her boisterous laughter. 

“All I’m doing is helping a struggling friend,” Cipher said innocently. “Trust me, Deliverer. You’ll thank me later.” 

With shaking hands, Phainon peered into the bag again. A hot pink box had the words Anal Fleshlight sprawled across the top, along with a clear window showcasing the product. Cipher had even been generous enough to provide him with a bottle of lubricant. 

“It’s a nice brand, too,” she said. She was clearly unfazed by Phainon’s angry stare. 

“This will be going right into my bottom drawer, and  won’t be touched until the next time I visit. And the first thing on our itinerary will be returning…this to the place you bought it from.”

“I won’t hold you to that. Don’t worry if you ever feel like changing your mind.”

The night sky was breached by the bright lights of the bus, bringing Phainon and Castorice’s day to a close. The two of them waited for the vehicle to stop, climbing up the steps when the door opened.

The bus was empty apart from the two of them and the driver. Phainon followed Castorice to the back, where they sat side by side. The door closed, and Phainon got his last glance of Cipher through the window as the bus drove away.

“Goodnight, Okhema,” Castorice said softly.

Chapter End Notes
