chapters.title: Chapter 7: Fall 16, Year 1
chapters.html:
Phainon hadn’t been on Mydeimos’ farm since their argument that Spring. 

It had naturally changed a lot in the past two seasons: he’d upgraded his coop, had a barn built, and nearly quadrupled the amount of crops planted. Wooden paths were arranged to create a walkway, with thin planks passing through tilled fields and past fenced-in animal homes. “I love what you’ve done with this place,” Phainon said, watching his chickens strut leisurely amongst the blue grass. 

“Thank you. I’m glad your opinion has improved since the last time you came.” Mydeimos had led the two of him to his front door, and was fiddling in his pocket for the house keys. “I hope you don’t mind the mess. I…wasn’t really planning on having anyone over today.”

The Valley Fair took place on the 16th of Fall every year; visitors from neighboring towns would come both to host booths and purchase wares from the town’s craftsmen. Phainon and Cyrene had been preparing for the main event-the Grange Display Contest-for weeks leading up to the event, but despite their best efforts, Mydeimos had taken first place.

While Phainon had not taken his defeat at the Egg Festival well, this loss was different. He didn’t see Mydeimos as just some city kid, but as a worthy opponent. The range of items at his grange display was wider than he’d ever seen: artisan goods, minerals, fruits, and home-cooked meals had all been arranged in a neat little square. Phainon had been the first person to tell Mydeimos that he deserved his win. In return, Mydeimos had offered to let him taste some of those award winning dishes at his home. 

Those award-winning eggs were from your chickens, after all, he’d told him.

Mydeimos opened the now-unlocked door, and took off his boots when he stepped inside. “What mess?” Phainon asked, following the other man inside. “It’s so…nice in here.” 

The best word to describe Mydeimos’ house, Phainon thought as he looked around, was cozy. The main living space was made up of warm wood tones and reddish furniture. Various items scattered about showed signs of life, and Phainon saw a cat curled up on a chair near the unlit fireplace.

“I’m glad you think so,” Mydeimos said, shrugging off his jacket and hanging it on the hook mounted near the door. “Make yourself at home. Although, I would appreciate it if you took off your boots. I’d rather not have mud tracked in my house.”

***

As it turned out, Mydeimos was quite the sentimental person. 

A large collection of framed photographs were hung up on the man’s wall: young Mydeimos with a blonde woman who Phainon assumed was his mother, a preteen Mydeimos hugging a fluffy brown dog, a teenage Mydeimos surrounded by a group of friends. Phainon smiled as he examined the pictures. “How long did it take you to hang all these up?” 

“Hang what up?” Mydeimos looked up from his cooking, then realized what Phainon was talking about. An embarrassed flush rose to his face .”Oh. Um, not long.” 

“Hey, there’s no need to be embarrassed,” Phainon said. “I think it’s sweet, actually.” 

Mydeimos sighed, immersing himself back into his craft. “You’re talking like someone who wants to be kicked out of my house before he can eat.” 

“You wouldn’t,” Phainon said sweetly. “Your secret’s safe with me, Mydeimos. Nothing wrong with being a softie.” 

The timer on the oven beeped, signaling for Mydeimos to take the tray out. Neither of them spoke for a moment, and Phainon set his focus back on the images. A lot of them were taken in the city, their backdrops being tall buildings and crowds of people. That environment had caused Phainon stress, but Mydeimos seemed anything but upset; he smiled genuinely, laughed with his arm around a friend’s shoulders. 

He broke the silence. “Do you miss living in Okhema?” 

“…I’ll admit, there’s parts of it that I prefer,” he said. “But overall? No. If I did, I would’ve moved back a while ago.”

”It looks like you had a lot of friends there, though.”

“I did. They don’t live there anymore, though.” Mydeimos opened one of his cabinets, taking out two plates. “Moved off to college a few weeks before I came here.”

Phainon stared at the wall gallery again. He found himself wanting to ask Mydeimos more questions, to know more about his life, but he had a feeling he’d already overstepped. “I see,” he opted for.

“Enough about that. I brought you here to taste my cooking, not to bring the mood down with sob stories.” Mydeimos set down two plates on either side of the table, adorned with what looked like a pastry. “Anyway. Had I planned this…visit beforehand, I would’ve made a proper dinner. I am quite the baker though, if I do say so myself.” 

“So that’s why it smelled so sweet in here,” Phainon said. “You have a sweet tooth?” 

“My pumpkin pie wouldn’t have beaten you out if I didn’t.” 

Phainon looked up at Mydeimos, shooting his smirking face a dirty look. “Krateros himself said it was a close competition. Don’t act like you won by a landslide.” 

“I was complimenting you, Deliverer .” 

Phainon’s eyes widened. Mydeimos had never referred to him by a nickname before. “Deliverer, hm?” 

He hoped his beating heart wasn’t as loud as he thought it was.

“Is it…not okay for me to call you that?”

”No! I mean, you’re totally fine. Don’t worry!” 

Truthfully, Deliverer sounded much nicer from Mydeimos’ mouth than it ever did from Cipher. He’d said it in a sarcastic context, but Phainon heard a touch of affection in the name. “You can call me that more, actually,” he said impulsively, the words spilling from his mouth. 

The unsure look on Mydeimos’ face evaporated, the cocky smirk returning. “Okay then, Deliverer ,” he said-it was so casual , like it wasn’t making Phainon’s head spin- “Have a taste. Tell me what you think.”

Phainon’s face flushed as he picked up his spoon. Mydeimos’ use of his nickname made him forget all about the food. He scooped up a portion of the pastry, and put it in his mouth. 

The moment it hit Phainon’s tongue, he was hit with a burst of flavor. The juice from the berries and the sweetness of the pastry melded into an overwhelmingly delicious taste. “You were right,” he said when he swallowed. “You are a good baker.” 

“Thank you.” Mydeimos’ smug expression had been replaced with a softer, more sincere smile. “I made this from blackberries I foraged from the Valley and milk from a Kaslanan cow.” 

Phainon just nodded, another spoonful shoved into his mouth. “It’s amazing,” he said between mouthfuls. “Where did you learn to bake like this, Mydeimos?” 

“I taught myself,” he said, taking a bite of his own cobbler. “Also, please. Just call me Mydei.”

The butterflies in Phainon’s stomach fluttered all the more fiercely. 

***

”So this is baby Mydei, huh?” Phainon pushed the open photo album closer to the man beside him. “Don’t be embarrassed, Mydei. Look! You were so cute!” 

The two of them had conversed casually over blackberry cobbler. Much to Phainon’s humiliation, Mydei noticed how his eyes kept drifting to the photo gallery on his wall. Do you really find my life that interesting?

You’re a city boy who moved to my little small town. Of course that piques my interest. 

After they’d finished eating-and Mydei had cleaned up the dishes-he’d handed him a photo album. The cover was worn, no doubt from many years of use, and Phainon could tell from the weight of it many pictures lied inside. 

Are you sure it’s okay for me to look at this? Isn’t it…a little personal?

I wouldn’t have given it to you if I didn’t want you to see it. 

“Don’t make me retract my offer, Deliverer,” Mydei said. 

“You say that, but you’re smiling,” Phainon replied. “Let’s see. If we turn the page…”

The blonde woman from Mydei’s walls greeted Phainon with a happy expression. He heard the man inhale sharply from beside him. So he was right. That is his mother. 

She-Mydei’s mom-was smiling while sitting in a grassy field, her son in her lap. There were a variety of snapshots: Mydei giggling, Mydei stretching his little hands out, Mydei crying, Mydei suckling on a bottle. Phainon felt the corners of his mouth tug upward as he flipped the page again.

“I didn’t realize they had fields like this in Okhema,” Phainon remarked. “So many of these pictures were taken outside, and there isn’t a skyscraper to be seen.” 

“They don’t,” Mydei said suddenly. “Have grass like this in Okhema, I mean.”

“Huh.” Phainon went to the next page. There were buildings in the background in the next set of snapshots, but from what little he could see, they weren’t the modern structures of a big city. “Okhema must have changed a lot in the past twenty years. It’s unrecognizable.”

“ Phainon ,” Mydei said, exasperated. “You cannot be serious.”

”What?” 

He sighed. “Turn the page again.” 

Phainon did as instructed, switching to the next set of pictures. His eyes widened as he looked at the captured moments before him. “That’s…Cerces with you. In the library.” He turned to Mydei. “You’re…from Aedes Elysiae?”

“I spent the first couple years of my life here, yes,” he said. “Well, unless you count the first month I spent in Castrum Kremnos.”

Phainon cocked his head. “Mydei? How many places have you lived?” 

“Just the three. And that’s if you count my birth city.” Mydei lightly pulled the photo album over so it spanned across both of their laps. “I don’t, really. I remember nothing about it.” 

“I’m sure if you want to talk about it,” Phainon said, his voice soft. “But if you do…I’ll listen.” 

“It’s a long story,” Mydei said. “I don’t mind telling it to you, but are you sure you want me too? It’s not a happy story.”

“As long as you’re sure. I don’t want to pry.” 

Mydei sighed, gently closing the photo album and laying it on the coffee table. “It’s not something I bring up often, but…I think it would be good for me to talk about it. That being said, I’m not exactly sure where to start.” 

Phainon wasn’t sure why, but he felt his hand move on top of Mydei’s thigh. If the other man noticed, he paid it no heed. “Take your time.”

It was quiet for a minute. The soft noises of the crackling fireplace and Mira-the name of Mydei’s cat, which he’d told Phainon during their meal-purring felt almost loud in his ears. Finally, Mydei spoke.

“Castrum Kremnos…has a dirty and dark history,” he began. “When I was born, a little over twenty years ago, the city had already mostly fallen to ruin. Kremnoans, though, have pride running in their veins. My mother begged my father to take her to a safe place to have her baby, but he made her stay.” 

“A month after I was born, the last of the Kremnoan people-those who survived, anyway-evacuated. Left with nowhere else to go, my father finally relented. He and my mother moved here, to Aedes Elysiae.” Mydei paused. “They weren’t the only ones, either. Krateros? He moved here along with them.”

“Mayor Krateros?” Phainon echoed. His hold on Mydei’s thigh had tightened. “I…never knew.”

“That’s because he never talks about it. The devastation of his homeland-our homeland-wounds him deeply.” Mydei paused, gathering his bearings before continuing. “Compared to the death-ridden Castrum Kremnos, this small town was paradise. Mom…my mother, I mean, was so thankful her son didn’t have to live in that mess. She never took that for granted.” 

“When I was two, she took one of her biweekly trips to Okhema.” Mydei spoke slowly. His words sounded pained, as if speaking them elicited physical harm. “She normally came back with lots of things from the city. Baby supplies, special snacks, even toys sometimes. But…this time, she never came back.” 

Mydei’s breath hitched. Phainon rubbed his thigh, an act of comfort he wasn’t sure if Mydei even felt. 

“There isn’t much to say after that. With the money he collected from her life insurance, my dad took us to the city and invested in starting a business. That’s where he put all his time and love. Not like he had any for me to begin with.” Mydei snorted. “Everything I know about my mother comes from these pictures and from what Krateros has told me.”

“I…”

“You don’t need to say anything. There’s no need for words of console.” Mydei leaned forward, taking the photo album back off the table. “You listening to me was enough. To be honest…I’ve been thinking about Mom ever since I came back here. And I’ve been keeping it inside for too long.” 

“Hey,” Phainon said. “Didn’t I already tell you I’ll be happy to listen to you? I didn’t say that for no reason.” 

“Yeah, I just…feel a little stupid about it sometimes.” He looked down, staring at the book’s worn cover. “I mean, I can hardly remember what Mom looked like without looking at a picture. So why am I mourning her loss so heavily? So many years later?” 

A tear escaped Mydei’s eye, streaming down his cheek and landing in a tiny puddle on the photo album in his lap. He wiped it away quickly. 

“It’s not the same, but Cyrene and I lost our parents a few years ago. I’ve thought the same as you when I think about them-it’s been a long time since then. So why does it still hurt?” Phainon looked at Mydei, still teary-eyed and vulnerable. “It’s only natural to miss people who loved and cared for you so deeply. Your mother gave you the only familial love you’ve ever felt. I think anyone in your situation would feel the way you do.” 

Mydei put his hand on top of Phainon’s, which was still resting on top of his thigh. “I feel a little bad dumping all of this onto you,” he said with a hint of a laugh. “I’m sorry, I just…I don’t like being vulnerable like this.” 

“It’s okay,” Phainon said. He moved his hand so he could intertwine his fingers with Mydei’s. He felt the other man jolt, but he didn’t object at all; he laid their conjoined hands where they’d been before, resting there as if it was the most natural thing in the world. 

With his free hand, Mydei opened the book back up, flipping to the page they’d cut off at before. “According to Krateros, Mom took me to the library every day.” He smiled. “She’d read me the same few books, and no matter how many times I heard them, it would always calm me down. Maybe that’s where my love for reading comes from.” 

“Did you have a favorite book?” 

“ Where the Wild Things Are. The exact book my mother held is still in the library. I checked the shelves for it when I moved here.”

He turned the page once more. Mydei’s mom was heavily involved in Valley life.  She’d taken pictures at every festival their little town held: scenes from The Flower Dance, The Luau, Spirit’s Eve, Feast of the Winter Star were all captured in stills. “Guess that wasn’t the first time you’d seen the jellies,” Phainon said, a picture of baby Mydei reaching enthusiastically for the fish in front of him.

Dream-Mydei all but screamed when Phainon picked up his pace, pumping the toy faster and faster. He imagined the sound their bodies would make together–the lewd slapping sounds as they met as one, the moans dragged from their throats as they made love. 

He shuddered, whining as feelings of pleasure rose and his thrusts became more erratic. He was getting close.

“Fuck, Mydei, look at you,” he said, fully talking to himself. “How does it feel? Being bent over, getting fucked by Aedes Elysiae’s golden boy?” 

Feels so fucking good! Dream-Mydei moaned, the imagined sound filthy in Phainon’s ears. Please, Phainon! I want more of you!

“How insatiable. I’m already fucking you so roughly. What more could you want?” 

I–Phainon–

“What about if I…” 

Phainon painted one final picture in his head; him raising his hand up, before slamming it down onto Mydei’s ass. The man in his fantasy wailed in pleasure, now-reddened flesh jiggling from the impact. 

Fuck, Phainon! I’m coming, I’m-

“Mydei!” 

His orgasm hit him quickly. He moaned satisfactorily as he emptied himself into the fleshlight, warm seed stuffing the plastic toy. Hot water from the shower head fell into his open mouth as he panted, legs weak as he recovered from the overwhelming pleasure. 

After what felt like forever, he pulled himself out. He grimaced as he watched his spend drip out of the fake hole, his fantasy replaying in his mind as the white liquid mixed with the water in the drain. He was…so rough just then. What was that?

***

Mydei and Phainon stood alone in the Town Square, woven baskets in their hands.

“Back to two people,” Phainon said. He conversed casually, as if he hadn’t spent his morning furiously masturbating to the man beside him.  “Just like before you got here.”

Castorice had made it clear she wanted no part in this year’s Egg Hunt. If you were competitive last year, I cannot imagine how much a bloodbath it’ll be this time around. I don’t have a death wish. You two have fun without me.

“But unlike then, you’re not going to walk home with the prize.” Mydei swung his basket back and forth. “I hope you’re ready to lose again, Deliverer.” 

“I’m not,” he said. “Because I won’t.” 

The start of the race was the same as it had been for the past two decades: Mayor Krateros announcing the rules, the small crowd cheering as the countdown began, and the sprinting at the sound of the whistle. Phainon and Mydei ran in opposite directions the moment it was blown, tossing colorful eggs into their baskets with maximum efficiency. 

Phainon dashed past the Saloon and into the Mayor’s backyard, collecting eggs as he ran. He had 8 eggs now–if he’d done the math correctly, he only needed one more to secure his victory. 

“Five!” 

Phainon’s blood ran cold when he heard Krateros shout. He only had a few seconds left to get the last egg, but there was no time to strategize. He had to go for the egg by the Sewer. 

He ran as fast as his legs could take him. The plastic orange toy sat nestled in the grass by the Sewer hole, the stillness of it seeming to mock Phainon. He all but launched himself, his hand outstretching as he grasped…

A muscular arm. 

He squeaked. In his win-driven stupor, he hadn’t even noticed that Mydei had his eyes on the same egg. When he’d jumped to grab it, he hadn’t landed in the grass, but on top of the man’s body.

“Hey!” He exclaimed, the Mayor’s whistle drowned out by his protest. “That’s mine! I got here first!” 

“I don’t think so. I’m under you. That means I got here first.”

“Nuh-uh!” 

A wrestling match began on the grass. If they weren’t currently locked in a competition, Phainon would be more worried about his blood flow. Their current position was quite precarious; if he were to pop a boner, Mydei would definitely be able to feel it. 

Right now, though? All he cared about was that egg.

He thought he heard the crowd shout–some cheering, some calling for them to stop. Faintly, he also caught the sound of the Mayor’s whistle, furiously repeating itself. But his situation with Mydei was louder than all of it: their heavy breathing as they tousled on the ground overpowered everything.

“It’s mine,” Phainon snarled.

“I already told you! I was here first!”

“Because you pushed me!”

“Did not!”

Phainon fought with all his strength, fully immersed in the battle for the egg. It wasn’t until a familiar hand grabbed onto his shirt and yanked at him that he realized the commotion they’d caused. 

Everyone was staring. 

“What the fuck do you think you’re doing?” Cyrene hissed. “Mayor Krateros has told the whole town no roughhousing during the tournament every year. Are you insane?”

Phainon bit his lip. The carnage from their little spat was evident; both of their baskets had been knocked over, colorful toys spread among the grass. With horror, he noticed the Mayor was walking toward them, whispers from the townspeople following him. 

“Mydeimos. Phainon.” He sounded tired. Phainon couldn’t blame him. “Follow me.”

The two men shared a nervous glance. 

***

“So? How harsh of a scolding did you get?” 

The TV screen reflected Game Over–one Phainon and Castorice had seen multiple times within the past hour. The man’s attention was obviously elsewhere. 

“All things considered, it wasn’t that bad.” Phainon set his controller on the ground to stretch his arms behind him. “Just a lecture about sportsmanship and emotional maturity. And then Mydei and I were assigned some community service.” 

Castorice whistled, pressing the A button on her own controller to return to the start menu. “Maybe Krateros figured that the public humiliation you put yourselves through was a worse punishment than whatever he could come up with.” 

“Tell me about it,” Phainon muttered. “Cyrene is going to kill me. I dragged our family business through the mud today.” 

“Hey, at least there’s no other animal supply stores in the town. It’s not like your customers can go somewhere else.”

Phainon groaned. “Try telling that to my sister. I think that’ll just make her angrier.” 

“Well, there’s another upside.” Castorice turned down the volume, so the Chimera Kart main theme didn’t drown out their conversation. “You were basically assigned to spend time together with Mydei, right?” 

“Right. Upside. Don’t make me laugh.” Phainon sighed. “We were assigned three hour sessions twice a week until mid-summer. You think I’ll be able to hold myself together for that long?” 

The look on Castorice’s face was nothing if not exasperated. “Phainon.” The expression on her was scary. He swallowed nervously.

“Yes?”

“Do I need to invite Cipher over to speed things along between you two? I’ve had enough.”

“If you do that,” Phainon said, “I’ll be assigned a lot more punishment than cleaning up trash. Because I will fucking kill you.”

“Have you ever considered that you’re killing me? Both of us?” The video game had been completely forgotten now. “Phainon, he’s into you too. Why are you torturing yourself like this?” 

“Because I have no idea what I’m doing!” It was a desperate, frustrated shout–if Phainon hadn’t already hit rock bottom earlier in the day, it would’ve embarrassed him. “Mydei’s mentioned he’s had boyfriends before. Cas, let’s be honest with ourselves. I’d just fuck things up.” 

Castorice stood up from the floor, fetching a box of tissues from her nightstand. He hadn’t even realized he’d begun to cry. “Phainon,” she said gently. “Mydei isn’t the kind of guy who would reject you over something like that.” 

He grabbed a tissue. “How do you know?” 

“Forgive me for being blunt, but it’s clear as day to anyone you don’t have any experience in romance. He’s been showing interest in you for months now. If your inexperience was a turn-off, he would’ve given up a long time ago.” 

“But what if he doesn’t know what he’s signing up for?” Phainon blew his nose, quickly apologizing before continuing. “He’s going to try and kiss me, and I’ll completely freeze up.”

“Remember when we were teenagers? How Cipher invited us all to play spin the bottle, and you sat out because you insisted you wanted your first kiss to be romantic?” She smiled. “Cipher teased you, and you looked like you wanted to cry, but you still stood your ground. I gave up my spot, too, so you weren’t alone.” 

He sniffled. “I can’t believe you remember that. Wait. That’s why you stepped out?”

“Your happiness and comfort mattered much more to me than a silly game. Either way, I know how firm you were about that back then. Give yourself what you want, Phainon.” 

He smiled weakly. “I…I know he won’t turn me away. I’m just making up excuses. Because as much as I want it, I’m also scared. I just…I really don’t want to lose him.”

“Phainon, do you need a hug?” 

He nodded silently, letting more tears fall when Castorice wrapped his arms around him in a comforting hold. She’d been his best friend for as long as Phainon could remember–been each others’ companions throughout every struggle, every life milestone. She felt safe. Phainon realized how badly his emotions were backed up. How good it felt to finally let it all out, and to allow himself to cry. 

“I appreciate you so much, Cas,” he said. “More than you will ever know.” 

“I do too. I’ll always be here for you.” She hugged him tighter. “And as for what I said earlier? Don’t worry. I won’t make Cipher get involved if you don’t want her to. As much as I think you should be honest with Mydei, this is your relationship.” 

“Thank you,” he said through a sob. He hiccupped. “About Cipher…I’ll think about it another time. I’m too emotional to make any decisions like that right now.”

chapters.html:
It wasn’t until the summer weather hit that Phainon realized why Mayor Krateros stretched their community service across the seasons. 

“I didn’t believe you when you told me Kremnoans had a reputation for brutality, but I think I understand now,” he said. It was miserably hot during midday, especially without any cover for shade. “There’s barely any trash around Aedes Elysiae anyway. What’s the point of this?” 

“It’s a punishment for a reason, Deliverer.”

Mydei spoke plainly, as if he wasn’t affected by the sun, but it was obvious he was also feeling the effects of the heat. He looked stupidly good drenched in sweat-Phainon kept sneaking glances when he bent down to pick up litter. 

He was lucky Mydei kept his shirt on. He wasn’t sure he would be able to hold his composure otherwise.

“Community service is supposed to benefit the community,” Phainon whined. “Couldn’t he have assigned us something useful?”

“…Such as?” 

“I don’t know! I’m sure he could think of something more beneficial than this!” 

A gust of wind breezed past the both of them, coaxing a plastic water bottle out from its position under a bush. It rolled to Mydei’s feet, who shot a smirk at Phainon before leaning forward to pick it up. “No trash in Aedes Elysiae, huh?” 

“Shut up.” 

It wasn’t until Mydei left to throw away the trash and Phainon wasn’t swept up in his scent that he noticed it-an earthy, yet damp smell, different from the man of his affection’s. Petrichor. 

“Mydei!” Phainon called. “It’s about to rain!”

“So? Are you telling me a lifelong country boy like you is afraid of a bit of water?”

“Yeah, well this lifelong country boy can tell this is gonna be a downpour.” He felt a few water droplets land on his arm. “I’ll be waiting it out in the Community Center. If you want to get drenched, be my guest.” 

The rain picked up quickly, escalating into what looked like a storm by the time Phainon got inside. He groaned in discomfort; his clothes were soaked, and the water in his hair dripped onto his face. “Just my luck,” he muttered, taking fabric from the hem of his shirt to squeeze it onto the worn floorboards. 

It didn’t take long for Mydei to cave. He burst into the entrance, and Phainon almost burst out laughing-the man was sopping wet. “What happened to belittling me for being scared of a bit of water, farmer boy?” 

“This isn’t water,” he snarled. “Why couldn’t your Aedes Elysiaen senses tell you it would be raining slime?” 

“Oh.” 

In the time it had taken for Phainon to get inside and situate himself under cover, the normal shower had shifted into green rain. The strange weather was a phenomenon unique to the Valley; as a lifelong resident, Phainon knew it was completely harmless. But to Mydei…

He was putting on a tough front, but Phainon knew him too well to be fooled. “Is the mighty Mydeimos afraid of a little green rain?” 

“What is with this place? Your chickens are blue, and your rain is green.”

Mydei ignored his teasing completely, confirming Phainon’s suspicion. He couldn’t help but smile, earning an exasperated reaction. “Just what are you smiling at?” 

“Oh Mydei. Were I a bit meaner, I would come up with some elaborate story about how scary this weather is.” His smile widened, to which Mydei only scowled further. “But you’ll be delighted to know that there’s nothing dangerous about green rain. The only lasting effects will be the abundance of foliage around the Valley after it ends.” 

His expression barely changed, but Phainon could tell the information gave him a sense of relief. “Okay,” he said. “I’m still not going back out there.” 

“I never said I was either.”

 Mydei sighed. “Do you know how long this…green rain is going to last?”

“No idea.” 

“Well, if we’re going to wait out the storm, we may as well sit somewhere nicer. The Chimeras and I have actually done some work restoring this place.” 

***

The Crafts Room was near unrecognizable. 

The once-matted carpet was restored to its fluffy state, texture soft under Phainon’s feet. Previously empty space now had furniture: a plush red chair, tables and chairs, and a shelf of board games. “You weren’t kidding,” he mumbled. 

“When will you learn not to doubt me?” Mydei closed the door behind them, the sound echoing in the large building. “Shit,” he complained, holding the hem of his shirt. “I swear that’s more than just differently colored rain. This is unbearably uncomfortable. Mind if I…take this off?” 

Phainon felt his throat go dry. To think he considered himself fortunate before; Mydei taking his shirt off outside would’ve been much easier to handle than this-stripping alone in an empty room together. “That’s fine,” he squeaked. 

He watched, almost entranced, as Mydei pulled the article of clothing over his head. Phainon had seen him shirtless before; he’d spent many moments on both of their farmlands in anguish, begging his body to lay low. It had worked then, but now? 

Mydei was right in front of him, his muscled chest in full view-and as much as Phainon willed himself not to, he couldn’t help looking at those red tattoos. He mapped them downward, fixating on where they disappeared under his shorts.

If there was anything he accomplished, it was not whining at the thought of pulling those down, too. 

“Are you done staring?” 

“Wh-what?” Phainon spluttered, his cheeks flushing to a deep shade of red. 

“If you wanted to pretend you weren’t checking me out, you could’ve made it a little less obvious.”

It had been a while since Phainon felt intimidated by Mydei’s gaze. At this moment, though, it felt like he was looking through him. Like he could read his inner thoughts. “I…don’t know what you thought you saw, but it wasn’t…I wasn’t doing. That.”

“Sure you weren’t.” Mydei frowned. 

“What’s wrong?” 

Mydei closed his eyes and sighed, as if debating something in his head before talking. “Why won’t you just be honest, Phainon?” 

Phainon’s clothes were still sopping wet, cold and clinging to his skin. It still paled in comparison to the metaphorical bucket of ice water that was dumped over his head. “What…what do you think I’m lying to you about?” 

“You haven’t been lying to me. You’ve been lying to yourself.” He stepped forward, and Phainon felt his legs tremble. He thought he might fall over.

“I’ve seen the way you look at me,” Mydei said, even closer now. “You’ve been sneaking glances for the past year, Phainon. I’ve watched you get jealous when I briefly mentioned a past boyfriend. But even when I’ve made it very clear I like you too, you haven’t…done anything. Why? Am I reading the situation wrong?” 

It was the second time Phainon had seen Mydei cry. The first instance was at the farmer’s house that Fall day, holding his hand as he talked about his mother. He’d shed tears both in mourning and in shame-he’d admitted expressing vulnerability was embarrassing for him. 

Which was why seeing him like this-tears pooling in the corners of his eyes, trembling with emotion-felt like such a punch to the gut.

“There were so many times I got my hopes up, thinking you were going to kiss me,” he said. “I dropped what I thought were obvious hints. And I saw your friends smirk at you when they were there to see it.”

“It’s not like that! Not at all!” Phainon reached out to grab Mydei’s hand, who accepted the touch wordlessly. “It’s…Mydei, I have no clue what I’m doing. And I’m afraid of ruining what we have.”

Mydei squeezed his hand. “…Is that seriously all it is?” 

“Yes?” 

“Phainon,” Mydei said, sounding incredulous. “I already know that.” 

“And that doesn’t bother you?” Phainon asked. “Actually, wait. How did you know?” 

“Maybe knew is the wrong word. It was more that I assumed,” he explained. “And it obviously doesn’t bother me. If it did, why would I have spent so much time trying to get with you?” 

Phainon looked around awkwardly, trying to avoid eye contact with the man in front of him. “But what if I mess things up, Mydei?” 

Mydei squeezed his hand. “You won’t,” he said. He spoke firmly. Surely. Relieved.

“It’s just embarrassing,” Phainon mumbled. The carpet under his feet suddenly seemed much more interesting; he noted the patterns in the material, making shapes in his head. 

“Phainon. Look at me.” 

He did. Mydei looked at him with striking gold eyes. That stare that used to make him feel small and insignificant, but now was anything but. It was as if he was being gazed at by the blazing sun—intense, yet warm. Mydei’s free hand cupped his face, thumb wiping away a stray tear on his cheek. “You won’t ruin things, Phainon,” he assured him. “I promise.”

“I’m sorry for hurting you,” he said softly. His blue eyes burned, tears threatening to spill. “I hate seeing you cry, especially when it’s because of me.” 

“I hate seeing you cry, too.” He smiled, gentle and wistful. “We’ve both been stupid, so how about we just call it even?” 

Phainon smiled back, leaning into Mydei’s tender touch. It was a complete juxtaposition from his anxious self moments before. 

“To tell you the truth, I really want to kiss you right now,” Mydei said. “But I really want our first to be special. Not…like this.”

Covered in slime after a trash cleanup. Phainon supposed that made sense. “I—yeah.” 

Butterflies had taken flight in his stomach. They beat their wings rapidly and ruthlessly, as if fighting to escape their cage. “Sorry,” he stammered. “I’m just…a little out of it, still.” 

Mydei chuckled. “What? Me confessing my feelings to you while my shirt’s off makes you nervous?”

“So you are aware,” he said with a mock whine. 

“Indeed I am.” Mydei told him, tone unapologetic as his hand dropped from his face. “The rain must’ve stopped by now. Let me walk you home.” 

***

Phainon had always loved the Valley after it rained. 

He bathed in the earthy scent of petrichor, stamping his boots into puddles to make light splashes. The sun would emerge bright and proud, sometimes a rainbow accompanying it in the clear sky. The warm rays shot onto Phainon’s back as he walked on the muddied dirt road, hand in hand with the city boy he’d sworn he’d hated just a year prior. 

“Looks like you’re going to have your work cut out for you for the next few days,” Phainon said. The oak and maple trees along the path had turned into their green rain counterparts, moss clinging to the trunks and piled at the roots. “Don’t worry, the trees will go back to normal. The foliage though…”

Mydei looked disdainfully at the ground, as if a glare would make it clean itself up. “How do you country people deal with this?”

“It typically only happens once every couple of years. Plus, the extra greenery is actually quite useful.” Phainon swung their conjoined hands back and forth as they trekked ahead, mud squishing under his feet. “Seems my Mydeimos isn’t as used to the rural life as he thought he was. Are you sure that you’re the one walking me home?” 

“Is this the thanks I get for being a gentleman?” 

Phainon giggled. “You gonna own up to it, city boy?” 

“…You were a lot nicer to me earlier, Deliverer,” Mydei retorted, though his tone held no malice. “And considering your house is right up ahead, I think I did a fine job bringing you home.” 

“Mmh,” Phainon said, squeezing Mydei’s hand. “Almost wished it took you longer. I…want to spend more time with you.” 

“Wouldn’t you rather spend time with me when we’re not sticky from the green rain?” Mydei smiled—now standing outside Phainon’s front door, they’d stopped walking. “Don’t forget about that kiss you promised me the next time we meet, hm?” 

Mydei insisted that he felt gross after the bad weather, but he still looked so stupidly handsome—Phainon almost couldn’t stand it. “If you can’t kiss me on the lips, can you at least give me a kiss on the cheek?” The question tumbled out of him before he could think better of it. Heat rose to his face in embarrassment.

“Sure I can,” Mydei said. “What’s the magic word?” 

“Are you—fine.” Phainon huffed. “Please.”

Reddened cheeks grew ever redder when Mydei got closer, leaning up just enough to press his lips to them. The kiss was short and chaste, but the spot the man’s lips had touched tingled after he’d already pulled away—Phainon dumbly raised his free hand to ghost over it, and Mydei just grinned. 

“I’ll see you soon, Phainon,” he said before turning away. The Kaslanan stood in place, hand unmoving until Mydei disappeared from view.

Weeks had passed since that fateful green rain. 

It had been one of the busiest summers Phainon had ever lived through: raising the abundance of young livestock, tidying up the excessive foliage, and making up for lost crops were all tasks that filled his days. But no matter how overbearing his chore list became, there was one thing that kept him going—-that promise Mydei had made him.

Mydei’s workload was no better, Phainon knew. Not only was he swamped with the responsibilities on his own farm, the Community Center had been fully restored—the townspeople whispered about it as if it was a supernatural phenomenon, but Phainon knew for a fact that his friend was the one behind it. 

Friends? Weren’t they more than that now?

Phainon gazed at where his and Mydei’s hands were connected. It was the last day of summer, and one of the most magical of the year. Phainon had a feeling that tonight would be the night—a suspicion only proven by Mydei’s shy behavior as they walked together to the beach. 

That wasn’t something friends did.

“Phainon! Mydei!” Castorice called their names when she saw them. “We’re over here!” 

Castorice and Cipher had planned a small bonfire before Aedes Elysiae’s official celebration for the Moonlight Jellies began. It was just going to be the four of them—Cipher had called it emotional support in their group chat when she’d told Phainon about the whole thing. 

“Cas! And Cipher!” Phainon called back to his friends with a wave, dragging Mydei behind him when he ran over to them. 

“Finally, you’re here,” the catlike girl said as the two men took their seats in the folding chairs that had been set up. Phainon couldn’t help but notice how close together they were compared to the girls’. “Could you do us all a huge favor and be even later next time?” 

“Hey, you told me you were starting at 7:30. It’s not my fault your bus came here early.” 

Cipher swished her tail in fake annoyance, though the movement was restricted by the chair. “Tsk, I get it. Too busy getting ready to impress loverboy over here to look after your best friend.” 

He will be by tonight, Phainon thought to himself as he grabbed the bag of marshmallows beside the folding chair. “You survived,” he said simply, before ripping the plastic open with his teeth. 

Castorice stared at him blankly as he took the bag remnants out of his mouth. “You know I brought scissors, right?” 

“What is this? Is it National Bully Phainon Day or something?” He reached forward for the roasting sticks—one for him, and one for the man beside him. “Mydei’s nice to me, you know. Why don’t you two take a note from his book?” 

“Mydei’s also been staring at your lips the entire time we’ve been talking,” Cipher said back. “Sorry that not all of us are desperately in love with you, or something.” 

Phainon’s face flushed, a sensation that only intensified when Mydei admitted to it. “Guilty as charged,” he said, as casual as if he were discussing the weather. The Kaslanan boy almost asked what part he was talking about—the looking at his lips bit, being desperately in love with him, or both—but no words came out. 

Like many times before, Mydei had reduced him to nothing but a blushing mess. 

“Ew, get a room.”

Mydei took the roasting stick from his companion’s loose grip, a fluffy white marshmallow already speared on the top of it. “You’re the one who brought it up.”

“Even rendered your dear Deliverer speechless,” Cipher continued as Mydei reached the stick out over the bonfire. Bright licks of flame seemed to curl around the marshmallow, darkening its white color. “Do you feel no guilt at all?”

“He’s known how I feel for weeks now,” he responded, eyes turning to meet Phainon’s. He felt heat surge through him then—less so from the fire, but from the look in Mydei’s eyes. They held a hungry desire, but also soft tenderness. 

Sorry that not all of us are desperately in love with you, or something.

Guilty as charged. 

“You’ve got a mean streak, farmer boy,” she said. “Here, pass me the bag of marshmallows, will you?” 

Phainon took the chance to break eye contact. He took a few marshmallows out of the bag before passing it to Castorice, who then handed it to Cipher. “Acting like you’re much better,” the quieter girl said. 

“Kaslana over here would still be moping in your messages if it weren’t for me pushing things along.” She put several marshmallows on her stick before tossing the bag back over to Phainon. “He should be thanking me, if anything.”

As loathe as he was to admit it, Cipher was right. Without her—and Castorice, for that matter-he didn’t know how long he and Mydei would have spent running circles around each other before realizing. “Alright, fine, Cipher. I’ll indulge you,” he spoke. “Thanks for being overly pushy and TMI to help me with my personal relationships.” 

Phainon knew that Cipher noticed the backhandedness of his statement, but she didn’t let it show. In typical Cipher fashion, she just smiled. “You’re very welcome!” 

The conversation around the fire should have been uncomfortable, considering who was in attendance. But the openness and playfulness of it made the nausea in Phainon’s stomach settle—Mydei integrated so effortlessly into his friend group. How much luckier could a man get? 

Time passed by, the summer sun setting to be replaced by a dark sky. The warm smell of a bonfire mixed with the scents of nature and the loud chirps of cicadas. It was a delightful and cozy sendoff to the season, topped off when Mydei fed Phainon a marshmallow right off his own roasting stick—a taste he savored, even if the sweet was near-charred. 

“I wonder who feels sicker,” Cipher murmured. “You after eating a charcoal-black marshmallow, or me after watching the both of you.”

***

The Dance of the Moonlight Jellies would never cease to amaze.

One of Phainon’s earliest memories took place at these same docks, around twenty years ago—his mom holding his young self in her lap, Cyrene and his dad on either side. He babbled excitedly as lights came from the ocean waters, his eyes still as bright as they were in adulthood.

You see those fishies? She’d said, voice gentle and motherly. We call them Moonlight Jellies. 

He’d reached his small hands out excitedly, fingers opening and closing around nothing. Jellies, he’d repeated.

Every year since then, Phainon remembered each annual event: when he’d went with his best friend Castorice for the first time, when Cipher had told him about her plans to move away. The Dance after his and Cyrene’s parents had passed away left an especially deep mark on him—their absence brought an obvious loss, giving Phainon an emotion he would never be able to forget. 

Last year’s dance was the first he’d spent with Mydei—and, coincidentally, the night Phainon figured out his feelings. The man beside him looked just as beautiful as he did the year before: eyes sparkling with pretty lashes, pink-tinted lips softly parted. Unlike last year, though, his gaze wasn’t solely focused on the ocean phenomenon. 

“You know,” Phainon mentioned after Mydei snuck another glance the man’s way. “It was actually at last year’s Dance that I realized I liked you.”

Mydei leaned in to press a kiss to Phainon’s lips—a feeling that had grown familiar over the course of their night together, but never grew any less wonderful. “See you soon.”
